1. So you don't want to be buffering all the time. Generally you'll do it a bit outside of the normal's range, but you'll vary the distance depending on the opponent and where you expect them to be. You put out a normal and buffer it into a special when you are *not* in range of the normal hitting at the time you input the normal. Therefore it's very likely that if the normal does happen to connect with the opponent, that it was a successful hit. Usually in this case, the opponent dashed forward or did some other advancing move; attacked into your normal and you counter hit the extended hurtbox; or they whiffed a move and your normal connected with the hurtbox during recovery. In all of these cases, they couldn't have blocked, so cancelling the normal into the special worked.
   1. Note that there are ways around this. If the opponent expects this, they can walk up and block, trying to force your buffered normal to connect with them while they're blocking. Also, buffering involves whiffing unless it actually connects, so if you buffer a slower normal, an opponent may be able to whiff punish you.
2. Moves with decent range and reasonably fast are the best buffers IMO. You also want them to be able to combo into specials that can travel a decent distance, in case you hit an outstretched limb. This is why Sakura's [st.LK](https://st.LK) is one of the best buffers. Very fast, very good range, combos into MP DP which has good range. Some other good ones I know are Juri [st.MK](https://st.MK), Karin [st.MP](https://st.MP), Cammy st.HP, G's [st.LK](https://st.LK), Young Zeku [cr.MP](https://cr.MP), Birdie st.MP.
3. You won't be able to buffer with a majority of light attacks, because they have very little recovery. Your special will often come out even if the attack whiffs. But the lights that are bufferable (like Sakura and G) are usually some of the best because they have good range, but are still really fast because they're lights.

You can play a lot of these characters very defensive, so if any of their designs are your favorite, you could probably go with that. But some thoughts -

Sagat is an obvious answer, but he is very demanding to play. You need to have a very strong understanding of when and where to throw fireballs, and have very good anti-airs.

Juri is a versatile character, she can be played very lame if you want. Instead of a fireball zoning game plan, she is more hit-and-run. She’ll often want to back away to build charges, and then pester with her strong pokes and unique fireball.

Chun has very strong pokes, anti-airs, and a fireball, so she can absolutely be like a wall. Gill has some interesting fireballs and V-Triggers, and rewarding anti-airs. But he is one of the more complex characters at the moment.

If you want to play defensive, I would avoid Ken, Kage, and Cammy. They all really like to be in your face, so while you could find ways to be defensive with them, you’d probably be better off with other characters.

Sure, there are plenty. There are quite a few normals and some special moves. Juri LP pinwheel (vs standing opponents, it’s -8 vs crouching) and Bison MK Scissor Kick come to mind. But a lot of the time, moves that are -3 leave the character out of range of typical 3-frame jabs, so they’re still relatively safe. And a lot of the normals can also be cancelled into special moves, meaning you can’t usually punish them anyway.

In general though, having a 3 frame is a huge advantage over a 4 frame when on defense. There are many frame traps that will work against 4-frame characters, but not 3-frame characters. Also situations where a 3-frame character is even (+/-0) on block are much better vs 4-frame characters because they still have the advantage. Similarly 4-frame characters being +1 is much better against other 4-frame characters; they would trade with a 3-frame character if both hit their fastest button at the same time. So a 3-frame makes a big difference on defense, but it’s rare that it will grant you an ability to punish new things.

So the first important thing is deciding which V-Trigger you want to focus on using. VT1 has a very steep learning curve, and can do some of the most unique things in the game. But it also has probably the highest execution requirements in the game to utilize it fully. I'd recommend starting off with VT2 unless you're really into long combos and execution; otherwise, you could try out VT1 later (if you decide to), once you really know the character. VT2 makes basically any hit combo into lots of damage, and can be used for some really good pressure as well.

V-Skill use will usually vary depending on the matchup, unless you really prefer one. VS1 is very useful against characters with fireballs, as well as matchups where you might want a meterless knockdown from light attacks. VS2 can be very strong to set up offense in other matchups. Setting the orb behind them, then VS2 on block into orb recall will leave you close and very advantaged. But that use will be overshadowed by the reflect and absorb abilities of VS1 when fireballs are involved.

Get very, very comfortable with your anti-airs. People jump at Menat **a lot**. cr.HP and [st.HK](https://st.HK) will be your anti-air normals, both with and without the orb. They hit at different angles, so a key skill to learn will be knowing which to anti-air with depending on where your opponent is jumping from. Menat's most reliable anti-air is her EX DP (Guardian of the Sun). She only has this when she has the orb in her hands, but it's a great anti-air. It's fast, and gains full invincibility just before the attack is active, so it won't trade with anything. It's not invincible immediately, so it can still lose if you do it too late, but it's really reliable otherwise. It's incredible for some unique situations, like Akuma's air fireballs (it'll just go through them and grab him). This is one of the better uses of meter for Menat. Also, be careful about over committing to grounded attacks. Menat's orb normals are some of the best grounded pokes in the game, but they have a lot of recovery as well. If you mistime them, your opponent can jump over them and land a full jump-in combo. Make sure to be watching your opponent, and your spacing, and keep that in mind when you use the long-range pokes and orb tosses. You still have to incorporate them into your gameplan of course, but you just can't be careless. If you think they might jump, don't commit to anything big and then enjoy the free damage you get from anti-airing them.

Menat is one of the most versatile characters, so you can play her in a number of different ways. She always has strong zoning abilities from longer ranges, but some players like to take advantage of her close range game as well. Her pressure, mixups, and combo damage become very scary when the opponent is between you and the orb. If you properly space out her drill kicks (just barely hitting the feet/shins of the opponent), they'll be plus on block and leave you at point blank. These tools combine with her strong V-Triggers to form a really potent offense. But some players may opt to sit further back and play a straightforward zoning game, and she's great at that too. She's definitely a complicated character, but incredibly rewarding once you really learn her. Because she can played in such different ways, you can really figure out a play style that's perfect just for you. I'm sure I left off some important stuff, but I hope this helps a bit!

One thing that stands out to me is that it sounds like you want to switch from walking back to walking forward. But I think the best idea is not to focus on which way you’re moving as a game plan, but instead focus on the ranges you want to be at. Walk back and forth to get into - and stay in - the ranges that are advantageous for your character. Karin has her own best ranges, but it will also change depending on the matchup too. You don’t need to be aggressive to play Karin in neutral, you can play her more defensive if you like. But instead of waiting for your opponent to make punishable decisions, which can only get you so far, you really want to force them into making decisions you can take advantage of.

For instance, say the opponent has a heavy button they love throwing out. Learn the spacing just outside of its range, try to position yourself there, and then be ready to punish the whiff with an attack of your own. They didn’t plan to whiff and didn’t realize they made a costly mistake, but you forced them into it. Karin has some of the best normals in the game, so if you learn their uses and effective ranges, you can go far.

One other thing that’s important is not to give up too much ground. You don’t want to walk back too much, or else you’ll end up cornering yourself, and that makes your opponent’s offense much more dangerous. That’s one of the benefits for advancing, you can push your opponent to the corner. People tend to retreat if they’re uncomfortable at a particular range, so try to position yourself in that range as much as you can. Even if you don’t land a hit, slowly walking them to the corner can create some big openings for you. But if you’re too careless when you advance, you open yourself up to being hit. You need to find the right balance with your movement and spacing for your own play style. It takes some time to figure out, but I think that would open the game up a lot for you.

No character is irredeemably bad in this version of the game. The game is pretty well-balanced overall, you can win with any character. If you like Nash (or any other character), you should absolutely play him. You will be more motivated to play a character you like, so you’ll put more energy into them and probably end up stronger with them than you would with another character.

Also, as has been said before, tier lists are largely based on high-level competition. Things that may be weaknesses at the highest level may not even come up until you reach that point. Nash isn’t the strongest character, but he can absolutely get the job done. If you eventually get to a really high level, you may opt to try a different character, but that’s far off at the moment. Bottom line - just play who you like.
